title: Part XVI and Annex C (the C interface; C++ interoperation)

found.group: G7: Part XVI (Calling C) and Annex C (C++ interoperation)

findings.title: The Retained token of a threads(creator)/threads(main) callback can end on another thread, ending a one-thread owner there
findings.program:
from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained
import std.thread
class Game:
    score: i32 = 0
    fn add_point(): this.score += 1
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `register_cb` was given")
    unsafe fn unregister(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(unregister))
    safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
fn main():
    game = shares mut Game()
    token = register_cb(fn() owns game: game.add_point())   # line 13: the block holds a `shares mut Game`, allowed under threads(creator)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns token: pass)            # line 14 BREAKS: `token` is judged Send (nothing visible is reachable from `Retained[ForeignCallback]`); it ends on the new thread: `unregister` runs there, the block ends, and its `shares mut` owner subtracts a one-thread count on another thread while `main` still holds `game`
    h.join()
    println(game.score)
findings.why: [FFI-23]: "its end unregisters the callback through `destroys(f)` and then ends the block" (no thread named). [FFI-21]: "`shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`". [THR-8] infers `Send` from "nothing reachable from it", and `Retained[ForeignCallback]` is one type for every callback, its state unseen, so the token is `Send` by inference; [THR-10] then accepts the capture. [FFI-33b]: "A callback's thread is the trampoline's to check" covers calls, not the token's end.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-23]` … A `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token is bound to the thread that registered the callback, whatever the callback's contract: it is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8]`'s list of thread-bound values names it), so handing it to another thread is `E7008` ("`token` keeps the callback registered on line 13 for C, and its end unregisters the callback on the thread that holds the token; keep `token` in `main`, or end it there before the thread starts: `token = None` above line 14"). Its end, the `destroys(f)` call and the block's end, runs on that thread, so a callback's state ends where it was made, and a `shares` owner or a `weakref` link it holds under `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)` is counted on one thread only.
findings.codes: E7008 (no shape: E7xxx); add the token to [THR-8]'s list

findings.title: A threads(main) callback holding a shares owner may be registered from a non-main thread
findings.why: [FFI-21]: "`shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`, `[FFI-22]`". [FFI-22]/[FFI-53] check only the thread that *calls* the callback ("`threads(main)` or `threads(creator)`, which the trampoline checks"); nothing ties the *registering* thread to the main thread. Under `threads(creator)` the two coincide by definition; under `threads(main)` they need not.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in `[FFI-21]` "`shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`, `[FFI-22]`" with: "`shares`, `shares mut` and `weakref` only under `threads(creator)`, or under `threads(main)` where the registering call is in code only the main thread runs, decided as a `static mut`'s readers are (`[STA-1]`, `[THR-20]`: not reachable from `thread.spawn`, from a job outside a scope, from a callback C may run on another thread, or from an export under `threads=any` or `creator`); elsewhere it is `E7015` ("C runs this function on the main thread (`on_main`'s `cb` says `threads(main)`), and `worker` may run on another thread (`thread.spawn`, line 18), so `log`, a `shares mut` owner of that thread, would be used by two threads; share the log between threads: write `log = thread_shared Log()` in place of line 12, with `lines` `guarded by` a lock, or register the callback from `main`")".

findings.title: Extends O1: a library's foreign call is checked only against callbacks the library can see; a dependant's kept callback changes what the library walks
findings.program:
# package sim, compiled once:
pub class Game:
    pub score: i32 = 0
    pub names: Array[String] = []
unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn poll_events()                 # no `no_callbacks`
pub fn tick(game: Game):
    for name in game.names:               # line 8: a walk of `game.names`
        poll_events()                     # line 9: accepted when `sim` was compiled: no callback `sim` hands to C changes `game.names`
        println(name)

# package app, which uses sim:
unsafe extern "C":
    @safety("`cb` and `ud` are a pair `register_cb` was given")
    unsafe fn unregister(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(creator)), destroys(unregister))
    safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
fn main():
    game = shares mut sim.Game(names=[String("ann")])
    token = register_cb(fn() owns game: game.names.push(owns String("bo")))   # line 8: C keeps a callback that pushes to `game.names`
    sim.tick(game)                        # line 9 BREAKS: `poll_events()` inside `tick`'s walk runs the callback; the list regrows under the loop's position: use after free
findings.why: [FFI-52]: "Across a package's edge, the callbacks a package hands to C … are recorded in its interface file (`[EFF-4]`), so a program that uses the package counts them at every foreign call" — the *program's* foreign calls; the library's own call on line 9 was checked when the library was compiled, against the callbacks it could see, and [EFF-4] records what a package hands to C, not what its foreign calls are held across. The set of callbacks C keeps is a whole-program fact deciding a package's code, O1's shape.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-52]` … A package's foreign call is checked against the callbacks the package can see, and the rest at the call of the package's function: a function's summary (`[EFF-4]`, `[EFF-24]`) records each foreign call without `@ffi(no_callbacks)` it makes, directly or through the chain of its calls, with the places it holds across that call: each parameter it walks, reads through a read-only name or changes through a `ref mut` name across it, and each `static` of its own. A call of such a function from another package is checked by the caller, who sees every callback C keeps: where a kept callback of the caller's program changes what one of those places reaches (through a link, a field or an element), the call is refused as the walk, read or `ref mut` use would be (`E3020`, `E3021`, `E3022`), naming the chain: "`sim.tick(game)` (line 9) walks `game.names` while it calls `poll_events()` (sim/game.em:9), a C function that may run the callback C keeps from `register_cb` (line 8), which pushes to `game.names`; register the callback after the call: move line 8 below line 9, or, if `poll_events` never calls back into Ember, mark it `@ffi(no_callbacks)` in `sim`'s declaration". Nothing in a library is refused for callbacks it cannot see.
findings.codes: E3020 (B2), E3021 (B3), E3022 (B1); a new summary fact in the interface file

findings.title: from(static) admits memory C rewrites on the next call: a read-only view changed under its holder, a data race across threads
findings.program:
from std.ffi import c_int
@layout(c) struct Tm:
    sec: c_int
    min: c_int
    hour: c_int
unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(effects=[], no_callbacks, param(t, borrowed, one), result(borrowed, one, from(static)))
    safe fn localtime(t: i64) -> ref Tm      # C's `localtime` returns one static `struct tm` it rewrites on every call; the overlay author read "lives for the whole program" and wrote `from(static)`
fn main():
    a = localtime(0)                          # line 10: a read-only view with the `static` region
    b = localtime(90_000)                     # line 11 BREAKS: the same memory is rewritten under `a`; the call changes nothing the summary knows
    println(a.hour, b.hour)                   # `a.hour` is `b`'s; with lines 10 and 11 in two scoped tasks it is a data race on `a`'s memory
findings.why: [FFI-11]: "`from(static)` … a view … into what lives for the whole program (`[LT-1a]`, `[LT-3]`)" asserts life, not immutability; [LT-3] gives such views the `static` region, which [STA-1]'s statics earn by never changing. A foreign call's changes are its `ref mut` and `MutSpan` parameters, so line 11 is not a change of what `a` views for [BRW-1]'s read-only promise. [FFI-15] has the same hole for `nul_terminated` results (`strerror`, `getenv`).
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-11]` … `from(static)` asserts two things: the memory lives for the program's life, and nothing writes it after the call returns, neither this function on a later call nor any other. A result that holds only until the library's next call (C's `localtime`, `strerror`, `getenv`) is not `from(static)`: it takes the lifetime word `copied`, under which the wrapper copies the pointed-to value before it returns and the safe type is the value itself: `T` for `one` where `T` is a `Copy` `@layout(c)` type, `CString` for `nul_terminated`, `Array[T]` for `count(n)` with a `Copy` `T`; `copied` on any other type is `E5002` ("`localtime`'s result is a `Tm` C rewrites on its next call, and `from(static)` promises memory nothing writes again; write `result(borrowed, one, copied)`, which gives `-> Tm`, a copy of your own"). The lifetime words are `from(this)`, `from(p)`, `from(static)` and `copied`; `ember bind --report` lists each `from(static)` result as the assertion it is. Cost table (§X.4): "`copied` result: one copy of the value at the call, nothing else".
findings.codes: E5002; a new contract word `copied` (needs the owner's word, as O2 does); one cost row

findings.title: An Ember class derived from a C++ base has no thread contract: C++ runs its overrides and deletes it on any thread, ending one-thread owners there
findings.why: [FFI-39c] hands the object to C++ ("`b` ends, upcast to the C++ base") with no `Send` requirement. [FFI-22] attaches "every exported function and trampoline" but gives an override no thread word; [FFI-39d] checks only "every change those overrides make". [FFI-17d]: "`owner="foreign"` makes a foreign `delete` end it", and [THR-20]: "A `drop` runs where the last owner ends", so the `drop` runs on C++'s thread. [FFI-33a]'s "no one-thread owner reaches C (`[FFI-31b]`)" is about exports.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-17d]` … `@ffi(trampoline, owner=…, threads=creator|any)` says which threads C++ may call the class's overrides from and end its objects on; the default is `creator`: an object of the class is bound to the thread that made it (not `Send`: `E7008` if Ember hands it to another thread), its thread is recorded at the hand-over to C++ (`[FFI-39c]`, one store), and the thunk of every override and the trampoline's destructor check, in every profile, that the calling thread is that one, stopping the program otherwise ("C++ called `on_click` of a `Button` made on another thread (line 16); its class says `threads=creator`"). `threads=any` requires the class to be `Send` and `ThreadShared` (`E7015` at the class, naming the field: "`Button.log` is a `shares mut` owner, which stays on one thread, and C++ may call `Button`'s overrides from any thread (`threads=any`); make the log `thread_shared`, with `lines` `guarded by` a lock"), and each override is then checked as an export under `threads=any` is (`[FFI-33]`, `[THR-20]`). Cost table: "a C++ override call or `delete` under `threads=creator`: one compare of the thread".
findings.codes: E7008, E7015 (no shape: E7xxx); a stop text for §X.4's table; one cost row

findings.title: An Ember function given to C as a bare extern "C" fn value has no wrapper that attaches the thread and no thread contract
findings.program:
static mut TICKS: int = 0                              # line 1: a module variable of the main thread
fn on_tick():                                          # captures nothing, so it coerces to `extern "C" fn()`
    TICKS += 1
unsafe extern "C":
    @ffi(effects=[], no_callbacks)
    safe fn set_timer(ms: c_int, cb: extern "C" fn())    # line 6: no `callback(...)` word; is a function-pointer parameter one a `safe fn` may have? ([FFI-10] lists scalars, `@layout(c)` values and contracted pointers)
fn main():
    set_timer(10, on_tick)                             # line 8 BREAKS: the host runs `on_tick` on its timer thread: the thread is never attached (no trampoline, no export), and `TICKS` is written by two threads
    while TICKS < 100: pass
findings.why: [FFI-21]: "A C function-pointer parameter accepts a capture-free Ember function (as an `extern "C" fn`)". [FFI-22]: "Every exported function and trampoline first attaches the calling thread" — this is neither. [THR-20] names "a callback C may run on a thread other than the main one", and the glossary's callback is one under `callback(…)`; [FFI-52] counts "every Ember function given to C as an `extern "C" fn` value" for changes, not for its thread. `E5069` refuses `no_callbacks` only beside a `callback(…)` parameter, so `set_timer` keeps the mark though the host calls back.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-21]` … A function-pointer parameter of a `safe fn` or of an overlay entry carries a `callback(…)` word, or the declaration is `E5002` ("`set_timer`'s `cb` is a function pointer, and nothing says whether C keeps it or which thread runs it; write `param(cb, callback(retained, threads(any)))`, or `callback(borrowed)` if C runs it only during the call"); an `unsafe fn` may take one with no word. **An Ember function given to C as an `extern "C" fn` value is an export without a name** (`[FFI-26]`): its C entry is a wrapper that attaches the calling thread (`[FFI-22]`) and runs it, and its body is checked under the parameter's thread word, `threads(any)` where the declaration gives none (`[FFI-33]`, `[THR-20]`: `E7012` for a `static mut` it reaches without its lock). `@ffi(no_callbacks)` on a function whose contract takes a function pointer is `E5069`, as for a `callback(…)` parameter.

findings.title: callback(once): whether it returns a token, what the token's end does after the one call, and whether the used-up mark is taken atomically
findings.why: [FFI-21]: "`retained` returns a `Retained[ForeignCallback]` token … and with `once` the trampoline ends the block after the first call" says nothing of a token for `once`; [FFI-52] speaks of a `callback(once)` "not yet unregistered"; [FFI-53]: "a `callback(once)` slot carries a used-up mark" and checks "the generation and the function's type in one compare", without saying that the mark is taken atomically for a `threads(any)` callback.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-21]` … `callback(once)` returns the same token, which keeps the block until C has run the function or the token ends, whichever is first: a token ending before the call unregisters the callback through `destroys(f)` and ends the block; one ending after it calls nothing, since C gave the registration up by running it, and frees the slot's record. * `[FFI-53]` … A `callback(once)` slot's used-up mark is taken with one atomic exchange before any of the callback's state is read, so of two threads calling it at once one runs it and the other stops the program with the second-call text; the block is ended when the call that ran it returns.
findings.codes: none new; the stop text of §X.4's table

findings.title: [FFI-35a]'s kept-by-C mark has no bit in [OBJ-1]'s header and no rule says which line sets it
findings.why: [FFI-35a]: "A class object given to a `retained` parameter is marked in its header as kept by C and never moves". [OBJ-1]: "An object carries nothing else for the memory model: no access words, and no flags but a `thread_shared` value's three marks". [FFI-11]: on a non-callback pointer `retained` gives "no safe type … the call stays `unsafe`, with a raw pointer", so the address reaches C only through unsafe code, and no rule names the line that sets the mark.
findings.proposed_text: * `[OBJ-1]` … The top bit of the type index is the **kept-by-C mark** (`[FFI-35a]`), so a type index is below 2^31; it is the header's only mark on a value that is not `thread_shared`. * `[FFI-35a]` … The mark is set, one store, by a call that gives a `retained` parameter a pointer the same statement makes from a class object (`register(ref_to_ptr(names))`, inside `unsafe:`), and by nothing else: a pointer made earlier or elsewhere is unsafe code's own obligation (`[UNS-4]`: an object handed to another thread may move). A marked object never moves: handed to another thread while a `weakref` link on this thread points at it, it stops the program (`[THR-2]`, verdict 114).
findings.codes: none; the stop text [THR-2] already gives

findings.title: An extern type (and an opaque C++ class) is Send and ThreadShared by inference, so two threads use one C object at once through const T* views
findings.why: [FFI-8]: "incomplete `struct` | `extern type S`, used only behind pointers", with no marker rule. [THR-8]/[THR-9] infer both markers from what is reachable. [FFI-2a] derives "`const T*` is a read-only view", which C does not promise; [FFI-40a] says it of C++'s `const` ("not an aliasing guarantee") and Part XVI says nothing of C's. [FFI-33b] gives `threads(creator)` for thread-bound types and no default for the rest.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-8]` … An `extern type`, and an opaque C++ class (`[FFI-32]`), holds what the compiler cannot see, so neither marker is inferred for it (`[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`): it is `Send` unless its contract says `threads(creator)` or `threads(main)`, so one thread at a time uses an object of it; it is `ThreadShared` only where the program declares it, `unsafe extend Ctx implements ThreadShared:` with a `# SAFETY:` note saying that the library reads one object from several threads at once (as `Send` is declared for a type holding a raw pointer, `[THR-8]`), an asserted fact `ember tcb` lists. A view of one reaching another thread otherwise is `E7015` ("`ctx` is a C object (`Ctx`, line 4), and two tasks read it at once (lines 14 and 15); C's `const` does not promise that `ctx_lookup` writes nothing: give each task a context of its own, or, if the library allows it, declare `unsafe extend Ctx implements ThreadShared:` with a `# SAFETY:` note").

findings.title: The object model of a trampoline class is unsaid: where the C++ subobject lies, what C++'s delete frees, and how weakref links outlive it
findings.why: [FFI-39]: "the importer generates a C++ subclass, the trampoline, which passes on … the virtual methods it overrides" — the Ember object's relation to the C++ object is not given. [FFI-17d]: "`owner="foreign"` makes a foreign `delete` end it"; [FFI-17c] orders destruction; [OBJ-1] fixes the header and [CLS-6] keeps the block "once no `weakref` link to it remains"; no rule says what `delete` frees or who marks the object ended.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-39]` … An object of such a class is one block: the header (`[OBJ-1]`), then the C++ base subobject (the trampoline's `this`, at a fixed offset every upcast adds), then the Ember fields. The trampoline class declares a virtual destructor, which runs the Ember `drop` and ends the Ember fields (`[FFI-17c]`) before the base destructor, and an `operator delete` that calls `ember_rt`, which marks the object ended and frees the block only when no `weakref` link remains (`[CLS-6]`); so C++'s `delete` of an `owner="foreign"` object does what the end of its last Ember owner would, and frees nothing itself. An `owner="ember"` object is ended by Ember as any object is, its C++ base destructor running last.

findings.title: A C++ reference result's lifetime is derived as "into the object", against [FFI-2a]; a reference to another object is a use after free
findings.program:
import cpp "tree.hpp" with (project="t") as t
# class Node { Node* parent_; Node& parent() { return *parent_; } };  class Tree { Node* make_child(Node* p); void prune(); }
# overlay: `fn make_child(p: borrowed one) -> borrowed one exclusive from(this)`
fn main():
    tree = t.Tree()
    child = tree.make_child(tree.root())   # a `ref mut Node` into `tree`
    p = child.parent()                     # line 7 BREAKS: imported as `ref mut Node` into `child` ([FFI-40]): the view keeps `child` viewed, not the parent it points at
    tree.prune()                           # line 8: C++ deletes the parent; `p` is held valid, since `child` lives
    println(p.depth())                     # a read of freed memory
findings.why: [FFI-40]: "a `T&` result is a `ref mut T` view into the object and a `const T&` result a `ref T` one (`[LT-1]`)". [FFI-2a]: "In **result** position a pointer's lifetime is never derived." A C++ reference is a pointer, and `parent()` returns one into another object.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in `[FFI-40]` "a `T&` result is a `ref mut T` view into the object and a `const T&` result a `ref T` one (`[LT-1]`)" with: "a `T&` or `const T&` result is a pointer result (`[FFI-2a]`): its lifetime is never derived, and the overlay's entry gives it a lifetime word, `from(this)`, `from(p)` or `from(static)` (`[FFI-11]`), under which it is a `ref mut T` or `ref T` view into what the word names (`[LT-1a]`); without one the method stays unsafe to call, its result a `*mut T` or `*T`, and `ember bind --report` lists it among the result-position pointers with no lifetime word (`[FFI-35a]`)".

findings.title: A std::function imported as fn(A…) -> R is "called as any other": its target is C++ code, so its call's changes and effects are empty
findings.program:
import cpp "bus.hpp" with (project="b") as b   # overlay: `@ffi(std_function) type Handler` for `std::function<void()>`; `fn handler_of(bus: borrowed one) -> owns`
fn main():
    bus = b.Bus()
    names = [String("a")]
    register_push(ref mut names)            # C++ keeps a kept callback that pushes to `names`
    h = b.handler_of(bus)                   # a `fn()` whose target is C++ code
    for n in names:
        h()                                 # line 8 BREAKS: [CLO-17] works out the call's changes from "every function the program can put there": none, so a C++ target that runs the kept callback is unseen inside the walk
findings.why: [FFI-17a]: "with `@ffi(std_function)` on its overlay entry, a function value of type `fn(A…) -> R` (`[CLO-3]`), called as any other, which owns its target". [CLO-17]: "A call through a function value makes the changes, reads and ends of every function the program can put there" — the program puts none. [EFF-3] gives `FFI` to extern functions only; [FFI-52]'s list of what a *foreign call* may run does not name a call through such a value.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-17a]` … A call through such a value is a foreign call: it carries every effect (`[EFF-3]`) and counts as possibly running every Ember function C++ can reach (`[FFI-52]`, `[FFI-39d]`), since its target is C++ code the compiler cannot read; `@ffi(no_callbacks)` beside `std_function` on the type's entry says it runs none. The value is neither `Send` nor `ThreadShared` (`[FFI-17e]`), and its end runs the `std::function`'s destructor through a thunk, which `ember inspect` reports (`[FFI-17f]`).
findings.codes: E3020 (B2) and the others [FFI-52] names; E5069 for a contradictory mark

findings.title: The C++ handle class exposes "the class's pub methods", changing ones included, with no attach and no thread check
findings.why: [BLD-FFI-5a]: "the header presents it as a copyable handle class of the same name with the class's `pub` methods". [THR-1]: "no owner changes a `thread_shared` value directly (`E7014`)". [FFI-22] attaches the thread for "every exported function and trampoline"; a handle's method is named as neither.
findings.proposed_text: * `[BLD-FFI-5a]` … The handle has the `pub` methods a `thread_shared` name may call in Ember: those whose summary changes the object only through its `Atomic`, lock, channel and `guarded by` fields (`[THR-1]`); the others are left out of the header with a comment naming the rule. Each is an export under `threads=any` (`[FFI-33]`): its wrapper attaches the calling thread (`[FFI-22]`), its body is checked as such an export's is, and its parameters and result follow `[FFI-31b]`.

findings.title: An export's type mapping and the C caller's obligations are unsaid: which view types cross, with what carriers, and an Ember enum C may fill with any value
findings.program:
@repr(i32)
enum Mode:
    Fast
    Safe
@unsafe(export("set_mode"))
pub extern "C" fn set_mode(m: Mode, ref mut out: Stats, names: Span[CStrView]) -> i32:   # line 6: an enum, a `ref mut`, a `Span`: may they cross, and as what C types? what must the C caller make true of `out`?
    match m:                                # line 7 BREAKS: C passes 7: no arm, no default
        Mode.Fast: return 1
        Mode.Safe: return 2
findings.why: [FFI-31b]: "`@layout(c)` values, scalars, opaque handles, `CStrView` and `extern "C" fn` may" cross; [BLD-FFI-5]: the C header "takes pointer-and-length pairs", so spans cross too, and neither names `ref mut`, `Option`, `MutSpan`, an Ember enum, nor a carrier. [FFI-8] makes an imported enum `@non_exhaustive` because "any value may arrive"; an exported one is not. [UNS-4]'s obligations (a `ref mut` reached by no other name) bind unsafe code, and no rule hands them to the C caller.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-31b]` … An export's parameters and result are written in the safe types of `[FFI-10]`'s mapping and lowered to the same carriers: a plain `x: T` as `const T*` (a scalar by value), `ref mut x: T` as `T*`, `Span[T]` and `MutSpan[T]` as a pointer and a `size_t`, `Option[…]` as a null pointer, `CStrView` as `const char*`, an enum as its `@repr` type. An enum in an export is `@non_exhaustive`, or the export is `E5015` ("`Mode` has two values and C may pass any `int32_t`; write `@non_exhaustive` above `enum Mode`, and give `match m:` an `else:` arm"). `ember build --emit-header` writes above each prototype what the caller must make true, `[UNS-4]`'s words per parameter: a pointer valid for the call, a `T*` reached by no other argument, a `const char*` NUL-terminated, a count that fits its pointer; a C caller that breaks one is outside the contract, as a C library is.

findings.title: [FFI-52]'s example declares `safe fn register_cb(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)`, which [FFI-10] refuses; the user_data witness and the callback parameter's Ember type are unsaid

findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-10]` … A `user_data=p` parameter is an ABI witness as `count(n)`'s `n` is: `p` is written as a raw pointer at its C ABI position, is absent from the callable signature, and the call supplies the callback's tagged number for it (`[FFI-53]`); a `safe fn` may name it. The callable type of a `callback(…)` parameter is `fn(P…) -> R`: the C function pointer's parameters mapped by `[FFI-8]` with the user-data one removed, a raw pointer among them staying raw (a lambda's body uses it in `unsafe:`); `thread_shared fn(P…) -> R` under `threads(any)` (`[FFI-22]`), and `once fn(P…) -> R` under `callback(once)`. findings.title: Nothing takes an object back after into_raw(): no from_raw, no runtime entry for C, so an object given to C is never ended; and ObjectPtr[C]'s markers are unsaid
findings.why: [FFI-54]: "`w.into_raw()` gives the address … and stops Ember freeing it"; [FFI-23]: `ObjectPtr[C]` is "the address of a class object, which `into_raw()` gives, with no count of its own"; [OBJ-1]: "Foreign code never reads it; it calls `ember_rt`" names no entry; [FFI-36a]'s `adopt` reads a foreign `destroys(f)`, not an Ember object's end; [THR-8] lists "a raw pointer" as thread-bound without saying `ObjectPtr[C]` is one.
findings.proposed_text: * `[FFI-54]` … `std.ffi.from_raw[C](p: ObjectPtr[C]) -> C`, and `from_raw[T](p: *mut T) -> owns T` for an `owns T` given so, is an `unsafe fn` (`@safety("`p` is an address `into_raw()` gave, taken back once")`) that makes the value owned again, by one name, so its end frees it as before; taking one address back twice is caught as adopting twice is (`[FFI-36b]`: at run time in every profile, and `E5068` on one local). A C host ends an object given with `into_raw()` with `ember_rt_object_release(void*)`, on an attached thread, which does what its last owner's end would. An `ObjectPtr[C]` is a raw pointer for `[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]` and `[UNS-1]`: thread-bound, and read through only in unsafe code.

findings.title: Extends O10: the tagged number is not non-canonical on AArch64 (top-byte ignore) when only its top byte is non-zero
findings.program: n/a (runtime): a slot number with generation 0x0100 gives 0x0100_0000_0000_0010; under AArch64 Linux's top-byte-ignore, a C library that wrongly writes through it as a pointer writes to 0x10, or to a mapped page for a larger slot, and does not fault "before writing anything"; LA57 x86-64 has the same for a generation below 0x0100.

findings.title: Where an `owns T` of a threads(creator) type keeps its creating thread is unsaid, and its run-time stop can fire only through unsafe code or C
